US EV Sales Sit at 6% While Europe Hits Record 23%
14 photos
Photo: Tesla
Electric vehicles currently enjoy a simply ridiculous 23.2 percent of the new car market in Europe. As per Motor Intelligence data, the US of A trails behind at 6 percent even though many of the subject electric vehicles feature similar tech specs and optional extras between the American and European markets.
September 30, 2025, can be considered a turning point for US-market electric vehicles, namely the day when the feds killed both the $7,500 incentive for new cars and the $4,000 incentive for used ones. Everyone spent that summer sprinting to the finish line, a frenzy that saw EVs hit 8.5 percent of sales that month.
By comparison, EVs made up 17.7 percent of the market in September 2025. A sizable gap, for sure, and the reasons for it go beyond the loss of incentives. Reuters correctly pointed out that European customers have more options than American buyers, including B-segment models aimed at ordinary budgets. More than 150 electric models were on sale in Europe in the first half of 2026, up from around 100 two years prior.
Considering that budget-friendly options can be purchased for less than €25,000 as of this writing, it's pretty simple to understand that affordability is of the essence on the Old Continent. Chinese brands have added more competition to the European market, bringing even cheaper alternatives that hinder legacy automakers like Volkswagen.
There's also the matter of countries that offer tax breaks. Considerably higher fuel prices than in the United States have supplied another nudge, making the prospect of ditching internal combustion more appealing. The American market, on the other hand, cannot make a similar pitch.
Photo: Tesla Worse still for electric vehicles in the United States market, the Trump administration has rolled back federal fuel economy and greenhouse gas regulations, reducing the regulatory pressure behind the EV push of many automakers. Tariffs and restrictions on Chinese-built vehicles, together with their software, have also made it harder for Chinese newcomers to enter the US of A.
For the time being, the perfect storm created by what is happening outside the United States and within it enabled hybrids to pick up the slack. US hybrid sales rose a whopping 23 percent through the first three quarters of 2026, accounting for 15.6 percent of the overall market. Looking at the bigger picture, they offer a better compromise for many prospective customers.
Promising better fuel economy than a conventional gas car without the need to plan around charging stops is the secret here. Used electric vehicles are finding buyers as well, with sales of used electric vehicles climbing 19 percent through September 2026. Reuters also notes that depreciation can make EVs particularly attractive, though battery health is a big problem for second-hand models.
Automakers are seeing different results, with Tesla US sales falling 14 percent in the first three quarters as opposed to an improvement of 29 percent for Rivian. Traditional brands have it rough, with Ford and General Motors recording 68 and 43 percent nosedives in the period from January 2026 through September 2026.
Simply put, the used market offers the best clue that America's appetite for electric vehicles is still there. With used sales up 19 percent, it becomes clear that American drivers are willing to go electric as long as the price makes sense.
